title: Acute ischemic stroke: an in-hospital stroke alert

banner.text: Thrombolytic given: neuro checks and BP every 15 min, BP below 180/105.

objective: Stroke, hemorrhagic and ischemic, and neuroendovascular interventions such as coiling and thrombectomy
secondaryObjectives: In ischemic stroke, establish the last-known-well time, score deficits with the NIHSS, and screen for thrombolytic contraindications

brief.situation: 10:20 on the progressive care unit. Bed 12, 67-year-old, 72 kg, admitted yesterday with community-acquired pneumonia and improving. At the 09:40 vitals the patient was talking normally and ate breakfast. Now the patient cannot get words out and the right arm will not lift. No anticoagulants; mechanical compression for clot prevention. Two peripheral IVs.
handover: At 09:40: HR 82, BP 148/84, SpO2 96% on 2 L, alert and chatting.
Now: HR 84, BP 196/106, SpO2 96%. Right arm limp, right face droops, eyes turned to the left.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Assessments examine the patient; orders and calls act. The stroke team, CT and the thrombectomy team take as long as they would in a hospital.
While you wait on something you can skip ahead; the skip stops early at an alarm or a result.
Partway through you are asked to write your plan. The case ends when the patient leaves for thrombectomy (or at three hours), then a debrief scores what you did.

CTA read about 25 min after leaving for CT.
Neurointerventional team and angiography suite ready about 30 min after the call.

then.log: Now hard to rouse, vomiting, complaining of a sudden severe headache before drifting off. Left pupil larger than the right. Much weaker on the right than before.

Awake. Eyes and head turned to the left; does not look to the right. Right face droops, right arm drifts to the bed, right leg drifts. Expressive aphasia: understands, cannot find words. Pupils equal and reactive.

effects.log: NIHSS {nihss}: gaze deviation, right facial palsy, right arm and leg weakness, aphasia. A pattern that suggests a large-vessel occlusion in the left middle cerebral artery territory.

plan.question: Put it together: is this patient a candidate for thrombolysis, for thrombectomy, or both? What has to be true first, and what do you watch afterwards?

parts.label: Candidacy
parts.criteria: Acute ischemic stroke with a disabling deficit, last known well 09:40 (inside 4.5 h), glucose normal, no hemorrhage on noncontrast CT: a thrombolysis candidate. The CTA shows an M1 occlusion with NIHSS 14: also a thrombectomy candidate. Thrombolysis should not wait for the CTA or for the thrombectomy team.
parts.modelAnswer: Thrombolysis and thrombectomy. Last known well was 09:40, not 10:20 when it was found; glucose is 128; the noncontrast CT shows no bleed; the screen finds no contraindication. NIHSS 14 with a left M1 occlusion on CTA makes this a thrombectomy case too. Give the thrombolytic as soon as the BP allows, without waiting for the CTA, and call the thrombectomy team as soon as the CTA is read.

parts.label: Before and after
parts.criteria: BP below 185/110 before the thrombolytic (treat it first), then below 180/105 for 24 h; neuro checks and BP every 15 min for the first 2 h; any worsening, headache or vomiting means a possible hemorrhage: stop and get a CT.
parts.modelAnswer: Bring the BP below 185/110 first (labetalol or nicardipine), then keep it below 180/105 for 24 hours. Neuro checks and BP every 15 minutes for 2 hours, every 30 minutes for 6 hours, then hourly. A new headache, vomiting or a worse neuro check means a possible bleed: stop the thrombolytic if it is still running and get an urgent CT.

bleed.narrative: Sudden headache, vomiting, a falling level of consciousness and a blown left pupil: a symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage after thrombolysis. The team stops everything and rushes to CT.

reasoningCriteria.label: Written reasoning: candidacy, and what must be true before and after

expertPath.text: New right-sided weakness and aphasia: call a stroke alert now. Last known well is 09:40, not 10:20. Point-of-care glucose.
Neuro check and NIHSS (14, a pattern that suggests a large-vessel occlusion). Thrombolysis screen. BP 196/106: labetalol 10 mg IV.
To CT with the monitor as soon as the alert is out. Recheck BP 5 min after the labetalol; start nicardipine if it is not below 185/110 or to keep it there.
Noncontrast CT: no bleed. BP below 185/110: tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg bolus without waiting for the CTA.
CTA: left M1 occlusion. Call the thrombectomy team at once.
Neuro checks and BP every 15 min, BP below 180/105; any headache, vomiting or worsening means a possible bleed. To the angiography suite about 30 min after the call.

bleed.headline: Symptomatic brain hemorrhage
bleed.body: The most useful kind of run to learn from. Look at the BP: before the thrombolytic it must be below 185/110, and after it below 180/105, checked every 15 minutes.

toThrombectomy.headline: To thrombectomy, on time
toThrombectomy.body: A fast alert, the right last-known-well time, glucose and BP before the thrombolytic, and the thrombectomy call the moment the CTA was read. That is the expert path.

toThrombectomyLate.headline: To thrombectomy, by a slower route
toThrombectomyLate.body: The patient got there, but something cost time or safety. Check the thrombolysis time, the thrombectomy call, the BP after thrombolysis and the neuro check gaps.

time_up.headline: No thrombectomy
time_up.body: A large-vessel occlusion needs thrombectomy as well as thrombolysis. The CTA result is the trigger to call the team.

scoring.modelReasoning: In-hospital acute ischemic stroke: sudden right-sided weakness, right facial droop, left gaze deviation and aphasia, NIHSS 14, last known well 09:40 (the last time seen at baseline, not when it was found). Glucose is normal, so this is not a hypoglycemic mimic, and the noncontrast CT shows no bleed. With no contraindication on the screen, the patient is a thrombolysis candidate, but only once BP is below 185/110, so the BP is treated first and the thrombolytic is not delayed for the CTA. The CTA shows a left M1 occlusion: a thrombectomy candidate, so the team is called at once. After thrombolysis: BP below 180/105, neuro checks and BP every 15 minutes for 2 hours, and any headache, vomiting or worsening is treated as a possible hemorrhage.

glucoseOnly.ask: While the stroke team comes: which result has to be known before the thrombolytic can start?
glucoseOnly.explain: Blood glucose. The 2026 guideline says to determine glucose before thrombolysis, because hypoglycemia can mimic a stroke. It also says an ECG and troponin should not delay thrombolysis. Waiting for platelets and clotting times is usually needed only when a problem is suspected, such as an anticoagulant.

source.cite: Prabhakaran S, Gonzalez NR, Zachrison KS, et al. 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: a guideline from the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association. Stroke 2026 (published online 2026-01-26). doi:10.1161/STR.0000000000000513
source.note: 4.6.1 rec 5: determine blood glucose before IVT; ECG and troponin should not delay IVT or EVT (COR 1). FLAG: the 'platelets and coagulation only if suspected' point is from the 2019 guideline and was not found in the parts of the 2026 text read for this case.

noWaitCta.ask: The noncontrast CT shows no bleed and the BP is under control. The CTA will be read in about 10 minutes. Wait for it before the thrombolytic?
noWaitCta.explain: Give it now. The guideline asks for thrombolysis as quickly as possible, avoiding the delays that extra imaging such as CTA or perfusion scans can add. The CTA decides thrombectomy, which goes ahead alongside.

source.cite: Prabhakaran S, Gonzalez NR, Zachrison KS, et al. 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: a guideline from the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association. Stroke 2026 (published online 2026-01-26). doi:10.1161/STR.0000000000000513
source.note: 4.6.1 (COR 1): avoid potential delays associated with additional multimodal neuroimaging such as CTA/MRA and CT/MR perfusion.

bpThreshold.ask: If the recheck shows 188/102, can the thrombolytic go in?
bpThreshold.explain: No. Systolic must be below 185 and diastolic below 110 before thrombolysis starts, then below 180/105 for at least 24 hours. Treat it, recheck, and give the drug once it is below.

source.cite: Prabhakaran S, Gonzalez NR, Zachrison KS, et al. 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: a guideline from the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association. Stroke 2026 (published online 2026-01-26). doi:10.1161/STR.0000000000000513
source.note: 4.3 rec 5 (COR 1): SBP below 185 and DBP below 110 before IVT; rec 7: below 180/105 for at least the first 24 h after IVT.

neuroFrequency.ask: While the thrombectomy team gets ready: how often are neuro checks and BP needed for the first 2 hours after thrombolysis?
neuroFrequency.explain: Every 15 minutes for 2 hours, then every 30 minutes for 6 hours, then hourly until 24 hours. A new headache, vomiting, rising BP or a worse check is a possible bleed.

source.cite: Prabhakaran S, Gonzalez NR, Zachrison KS, et al. 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: a guideline from the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association. Stroke 2026 (published online 2026-01-26). doi:10.1161/STR.0000000000000513
source.note: Table 7: measure BP and perform neurological assessments every 15 min during and after IVT for 2 h, then every 30 min for 6 h, then hourly until 24 h.
